title: Home Affordability Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Home Affordability Calculator: How much house can you afford? Max price from income, debts, down payment and rate. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it,…
content:
The [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. How much house can you afford? Max price from income, debts, down payment and rate. Enter your gross annual income, monthly debt payments, down payment saved, mortgage rate and mortgage term and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Work out the most expensive home you can reasonably afford from your income, existing debts, down payment and the mortgage rate. The calculator uses the standard 28/36 rule that lenders use as a guide: housing costs should be no more than 28% of your gross monthly income, and all debts including housing no more than 36%. Whichever limit is lower sets your maximum monthly payment, and that payment sets the maximum loan — add your down payment and you have the maximum home price.

## How to use the Home Affordability Calculator

Start by entering your gross annual income, then entering your monthly debt payments, entering your down payment saved, entering your mortgage rate (%) and finally entering your mortgage term (years). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your gross annual income before tax.
2. Enter your other monthly debt payments — car, cards, student loans.
3. Enter your down payment and the mortgage rate and term.
4. Read the maximum monthly payment, mortgage and home price.

## Formula

Max payment = min(28% of gross monthly income, 36% of gross monthly income − monthly debts). Max loan = payment × (1 − (1 + r)^−n) ÷ r. Max price = max loan + down payment.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. On $100,000 of income with $500 a month of other debts, $50,000 saved and a 6.5% 30-year mortgage: 28% of monthly income is $2,333.33 and the 36% limit leaves $2,500 after debts, so the payment cap is $2,333.33. That supports a $369,158.58 mortgage and a $419,158.58 home. Try the same figures in the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Gross annual income: 100000, Monthly debt payments: 500, Down payment saved: 50000, Mortgage rate: 6.5 %, Mortgage term: 30 years), the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) returns Maximum monthly housing payment: $2,333.33, 28% of gross monthly income: $2,333.33, 36% debt limit less your debts: $2,500, Maximum mortgage: $369,158.58, Maximum home price: $419,158.58. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## The 28/36 rule

Lenders traditionally like two ratios: the front-end ratio (housing costs ÷ gross income) at 28% or below, and the back-end ratio (all debts including housing ÷ gross income) at 36% or below. Some lenders accept up to 43% or even 50% on the back-end ratio, especially for strong credit — but borrowing to the absolute maximum leaves no room for repairs, rate rises or a lost income. The 28/36 rule is a guide to comfortable affordability, not a lender's final word.

## What this leaves out

The payment here is principal and interest only. A lender's real housing figure also includes property tax, homeowner's insurance and PMI if the down payment is under 20%, which can add hundreds a month. It also ignores your credit score, which sets the rate you are actually offered, and your cash reserves. Use the result as a ceiling to shop under, not a target to hit.

## Debts matter as much as income

Because the 36% limit counts all debts, paying off a car loan or a credit card before house-hunting can raise the home you can afford more than a pay rise of the same size. Every $100 of monthly debt you remove frees up roughly $100 of monthly mortgage payment — about $16,000 of home price at current rates.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Shop below the maximum — the calculator's number is a ceiling, not a goal.
- Paying down monthly debts before applying raises your affordable price.
- Remember tax, insurance and PMI sit on top of the principal-and-interest payment shown here.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much house can I afford on $100,000 a year?

By the 28/36 rule, about $2,333 a month of housing payment, which at 6.5% over 30 years supports roughly a $419,000 home with $50,000 down. Your debts and credit score move that number up or down. Try it with your own numbers in the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the 28/36 rule?

A lending guideline: housing costs at most 28% of gross monthly income, and all debts including housing at most 36%. It is a comfort guide — some lenders allow higher ratios, but higher ratios leave less room for everything else. Try it with your own numbers in the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does a bigger down payment mean a more expensive house?

Yes, dollar for dollar: the maximum home price is the maximum mortgage plus your down payment. A bigger down payment also cuts the monthly payment, the interest paid and usually removes PMI. Try it with your own numbers in the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Home Affordability Calculator use?

Max payment = min(28% of gross monthly income, 36% of gross monthly income − monthly debts). Max loan = payment × (1 − (1 + r)^−n) ÷ r. Max price = max loan + down payment. You can see it in action in the [Home Affordability Calculator](/home-affordability-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
